title: Good time to come back to game dev?
author: Mekanofreak
selftext:
I have an honest question, and since ai is heavily involved, I felt this sub was a good place to have this discussion.

I spent years making small game project, lots of ideas on paper, but I never actually published anything. I made a few finished prototypes, some small game to learn, did a few non-gaming related coding project for work (I'm not in the tech industry at all, I work a trade job). 

As for my abilities, I dabbled in coding for a while as a hobby (learned unity script, then c#) , learned blender and even made some attempts at drawing and pixel art. The only thing I consider myself good at is writing (not in English mind you, it's not my first language.) I wrote many short stories and always received good reviews for them. 

The main reason I never made one of my *dream* games (I know this word is thrown around a lot, but bear with me I don't know how to describe it any other way) was always a lack of ressources (Day job not making enough to feed my family AND pay an artist for the art) , lack of time due to my day job or family, and sometime, my inability to actually code what I wanted in the game, and admittedly some scope creep and a bit of misplaced perfectionism. 

Now, I see what people use AI for, and to be frank, I used to be a bit anti AI, but am realising, like many other I believe, it's potential as a tool. I don't think it's a magic thing where you put a few words in and get your *perfect* project out, I've seen the "slop" games that are flooding the net. I know there's still a lot of work involved, but, as someone who's average at all aspect of making games exept maybe writing, do you think it's a good time to get back into it, learn to use AI to try and help my shortcoming and try to finally get some of those ideas out my head?

comments.author: tabaxi_gf
comments.body: Why not?  It’s very easy to learn how to make any software with ai. I would recommend starting small however. You can always build a prototype out.

comments.author: Manifesto-Engine
comments.body:
Yes. AI is reallyy useful for this now, especially if you already have ideas and some programming experience. Claude Opus 5.5 has been extremely capable for game development in my experience, but the biggest thing I’ve learned is not to just prompt “make my game.”

Start by building **editors and tools** for the parts you care about. Make an editor that establishes your art direction, another for creatures/items/worlds/levels, whatever your game needs. Then you’re giving the AI actual systems and constraints to build around instead of asking it to invent everything from scratch every time.

Keep the scope small at first, play what it makes constantly, and treat the AI like a very fast developer you still have to direct and review. You’ll absolutely still hit bugs, bad architecture, weird design decisions, and scope creep.

But for someone who has ideas sitting around because art, coding time, or implementation skill was the bottleneck? I think this is probably one of the best times to try again.

replies.author: Mekanofreak
replies.body:
I already started working out how to work with vscode and co-pilot a few days ago. Started messing with the AI to make just a simple prototype, and I'm impressed so far the ability to just ask the AI questions on how to set everything up also greatly helped. I haven't tried Claude code yet, I'm used to coding in either notepad++ and vscode for my unity projects back in the days, so that's why I'm using it, and a copilot Github pro subscription was only 10 bucks and it's plenty for my test so far. 

I'm, also learning comfyui on the side at the same time for some prototype artwork.

replies.author: liatris4405
replies.body:
This is just my personal opinion, but honestly, since I hardly ever write code by hand anymore, I think knowing the basics of tools like VS Code is enough. It helps to at least know where to click to view the code.

If you’re going to learn programming, I’d put more emphasis on software design: things like understanding why it’s a good idea to separate data from code from the start, or how the project’s folders are organized. AI can handle most of this, but knowing enough to work through those details with it at the beginning can significantly reduce development time.

replies.author: Mekanofreak
replies.body:
As mentionned, I'm no stranger to programming and I think I have a good enoug grasp on the basics. I'm used to keeping my projects organized... In fact, probably overly so, I end up with too many folders and often ended up separating scripts on top many files 😅 , that's how I learned unity tough, keeping everything separate so it's easily modifiable, fixable and modular. Don't know how that way of doing things will translate to working with the ai.

I do like to think I know enoug to understand the code the ai will write and find some mistakes, but I'm a bit rusty, her a bit over a year since my last coding project and it was only a simple software for searching a database of tools at my work. 

I worked with renpy on visual novels before too, and always tried splitting my code for text effects, minigames, variables, ect, separate from the actual story, not because of localisation, mainly because that's how I learned it from others, but your explanation make sense for translation.

comments.author: Significant-Neck-520
comments.body: If you want to have comercial success, things are really hard right now due to how much things are being produced. But if you want to produce a game, AI can help a ton, yes.

replies.author: Mekanofreak
replies.body: Ho, I'm not hoping to have any Sucess, or publish them even. I never considered game making as anything other than a hobby for me. Mainly I'd like to get those ideas and stories out of my head. I don't have any crazy ideas that what I can produce would make it on the market, especially with all the awesome games both ai and no-ai devs are making.

replies.author: Significant-Neck-520
replies.body: Yeah, it is still not perfect graphics wise, but there is a lot of programming that can be done quickly. You get to see your idea working without having to work many hours until reaching that stage. Just describe the ideas in detail, and the AI can figure it out

I can't code and I'm not in tech, and in the last week and a half I made two phone games with Claude, no artist either, all the graphics are drawn by code. what helped me most with scope creep and perfectionism: before anything gets built I ask for 2 or 3 rough versions, pick one and move on. and finish something tiny first, then grow it. also use it to talk things through, not only to write code, a lot of my best decisions came out of just discussing the problem first

comments.author: Fuzz-Monster
comments.body: If it's for fun then sure. If you're seeking to make a living, maybe not. It's always been very challenging to get eyeballs on your game and it's getting exponentially harder now with the deluge of products from AI-enabled creators.

replies.author: Mekanofreak
replies.body: As I said in another answer, it's a hobby, I don't believe I'd be able to make anything that would compete with what indie dev are making, ai or not. Mainly want to have fun and get a few story and ideas and concepts out of my head that I had for years.

comments.body:
define "good time"

"I don't think it's a magic thing where you put a few words in and get your *perfect* project out," AI is getting close to that. if you wait until 2027/2028... it may just be... that. 

I mean, I am not sure why you need second opinions when AI access is free. it is not some huge commitment. 

its like you find the door but you decide to stop right before the door and ask "should I open the door? guys?" 

if you lack the basic motivation to even experiment AI gamedev yourself, I am not sure what we said would matter to you.

replies.author: Mekanofreak
replies.body:
I already started experimenting, so no, no lack of motivation, I don't know where you see that In my post. So no, haven't stoped in front of the door and asked if I should open it. 

I define *good time* exactly as others (all helpfull comments by the way) have told me : "yes, the tools are there, it's working for us, it's a good time". I I had received comments like "no it's not ready, the tools are lacking for now, ect" I would have tought about it.

Aldo, define "free". Because just testing things, I went over the free limit of 3 providers and finally signed up for one of them, not costing a lot, mind you, but your free might not be my free.

Also, might not be a huge commitment for you, but as a father of multiple kids, a husband, the owner of multiples dogs and other interests and with a full time job, my free time is limited, so using it to go back to this, instead of another hobby is a commitment for me. Still, thank you for your opinion.

I appreciate all the comments I received so far, I asked to get opinions, that's what a conversation is for.

replies.body:
I meant "free" as in "it is free". there are permanent free options without usage limits if you look. If you had asked me before you pay for a subscription, I would caution you to experiment more before you start paying.

anyway, since you already started and you are paying for a subscription already, not sure what else you need to hear. 

if you really want to be time efficient, then you can technically save your big idea until 2027. The most recent couple upgrades already made gamedev very easy. So it is only getting easier over time. 

so maybe focus your time on getting used to AI and only work on a big game when AI feels smart enough for you.

Also, if you read my posts, there's no "big idea" just normal ideas and things I want to get out of my head. I'm not doing this hoping for Sucess, money or recognition. 

Without realising it, your answers are in fact leaning me toward the "Yes it might be as good a time as any". Even if if you sound a bit rough around the edges. So again, thank you for the conversation.

comments.author: CycleMother2006
comments.body:
AI pairs well with human effort. We're very, very far still from a reasonable game being spit out in one prompt, and even if we do ever arrive there, it will only be made better by effort and clear direction. Where I'm finding its real magic is is in setting up incredible foundations. You can really perform optimizations that would take months or years of study to properly understand and implement in your game. You want ray tracing? Great, you can do it, and you can even do it efficiently and in smart ways rather than just throwing your graphics card at it in a half-assed way. You want to incorporate nanite for beautiful distant landscapes? Go ahead.

Ignore the lights and colors and flashiness of some of these one shots. They veil all the inconsistent styling and poorly made assets underneath. There are fantastic AI-development driven games right now but they're ongoing projects that are many months in development. 

AI can let you do it though. But it's going to take a LOT of hours from you. I spent 3 days developing clouds and the overall sky for my game because i wanted a very specific look that no other game had done (at least to my knowledge). That's roughly 20 hours brainstorming, mocking up, testing, working out shaders, handmodeling, testing some more, smoothing performance, adjusting animations and wind, tweaking shaders, etc. Because I didn't want to accept generic slop clouds which it otherwise would've spit out and resembled the same puffs or skyboxes you see in every other stylistic 3d ai production.

So depending on the quality you're looking for for your dream game, you may still dump thousands of hours into the project. But you will get a return from it as long as you can communicate your intent. Without manually learning modeling, art direction, etc, I'd temper your expectations a bit. But with enough AI iteration you might be able to cover some of those gaps. If your vision isn't crystal clear and more... open to interpretation, you'll probably respond better to the results. Getting 70% of the way there is 10x easier than getting 100% of what you want, so just having a rough idea in your head instead of a clearly defined end game does mean more satisfaction later (though also worse results).
